clinicalPearls: A rare pancreatic alpha-cell neuroendocrine tumour that secretes excess glucagon
The characteristic rash, necrolytic migratory erythema, is a migratory, crusting, erosive eruption favouring the perineum, groin, and extremities
Other typical features include weight loss, a sore red tongue and angular stomatitis, mild diabetes or glucose intolerance, and normocytic anaemia
There is an increased risk of venous thromboembolism, which contributes to morbidity
Diagnosis rests on a markedly elevated fasting plasma glucagon level together with the clinical syndrome
The rash may respond partly to correction of associated amino acid, zinc, and fatty acid deficiencies as well as to control of the tumour
Many tumours are large and a substantial proportion have metastasised, usually to the liver, by the time of diagnosis, so imaging for localisation and staging is essential
Consider a possible association with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1, and manage with somatostatin analogues for symptom control and surgery for resectable disease
reference.pathophysiology: A glucagonoma is a functioning neuroendocrine tumour of pancreatic alpha cells that oversecretes glucagon. Glucagon is a catabolic, counter-regulatory hormone that promotes hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, causing hyperglycaemia, and stimulates lipolysis and amino acid catabolism, leading to weight loss and depletion of circulating amino acids. The resulting hypoaminoacidaemia, together with deficiencies of zinc and essential fatty acids, is thought to underlie necrolytic migratory erythema. Glucagon excess also promotes a prothrombotic state. Because symptoms are non-specific and evolve slowly, diagnosis is often delayed until the tumour is large or metastatic, most commonly to the liver.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of necrolytic migratory erythema-like rashes such as zinc deficiency (acrodermatitis)
Type 2 diabetes mellitus with weight loss
Chronic liver disease with skin and nutritional changes
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count for normocytic anaemia and serum zinc and amino acid profile
Skin biopsy of the rash when the diagnosis is uncertain
Cross-sectional imaging of the pancreas and liver for localisation and staging
Somatostatin-receptor functional imaging and screening for MEN1 where indicated
redFlags: Venous thromboembolism, including pulmonary embolism, from the prothrombotic state
Extensive or infected necrolytic migratory erythema
Metastatic disease, most often hepatic, at presentation
Profound catabolism with severe weight loss and malnutrition
reference.prognosis: Complete resection of localised disease can be curative and reverses the syndrome, but many patients present with metastatic disease; even then, these tumours are often relatively indolent and symptoms can be controlled for prolonged periods with somatostatin analogues and other systemic therapy.
pitfalls: Treating recurrent necrolytic migratory erythema as a primary dermatosis and missing the underlying tumour
Attributing new diabetes with weight loss solely to typical type 2 diabetes
Overlooking thromboprophylaxis needs given the high thrombotic risk
Failing to correct nutritional deficiencies that perpetuate the rash
management: Surgical resection of localised tumour, which can be curative and reverses the syndrome
Somatostatin analogues such as octreotide or lanreotide to suppress glucagon secretion, control the necrolytic migratory erythema and slow tumour progression
Correct associated amino acid, zinc and essential fatty acid deficiencies to improve the rash, and manage the diabetes or glucose intolerance
Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis or anticoagulation given the prothrombotic state
For metastatic disease use liver-directed therapy, peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, or targeted agents such as everolimus or sunitinib
Monitor fasting glucagon, glycaemic control and cross-sectional imaging for tumour response and progression
Screen for MEN1 and offer genetic counselling where indicated, coordinating care through a neuroendocrine tumour multidisciplinary team
